q: How do migratory birds know exactly where to go every year?
How do birds know where to migrate?
How do birds find their way during migration?
a: Migratory birds navigate using a combination of celestial cues, Earth's magnetic field, visual landmarks, and innate biological mechanisms. Birds use the position of the sun during the day as a compass, compensating for its movement across the sky by using their internal circadian clock. At night, many species navigate by the stars, with the North Star and other constellations serving as reference points. Most remarkably, birds can detect Earth's magnetic field through specialized cells containing a protein called cryptochrome in their eyes, which allows them to 'see' magnetic fields as visual patterns. Some birds also use polarized light patterns in the sky, which are invisible to humans but provide directional information. Young birds often inherit their migratory routes genetically — they know when and where to go without being taught. Experiments have shown that birds raised in isolation will still attempt to migrate in the correct direction at the right time. Birds also use visual landmarks like coastlines, rivers, and mountain ranges during migration. Some species fly thousands of miles non-stop, such as the Arctic Tern which travels from the Arctic to Antarctica and back each year. The combination of these navigation systems — magnetic, celestial, visual, and innate — allows birds to undertake some of the most remarkable journeys in the natural world, often returning to the exact same nesting sites year after year.
